tier_reason: The may_minihttp README Performance section shows the author's own wrk runs (-d 10 -t 1 -c 200, one worker thread, 'my laptop'): tokio_minihttp 100650.94 req/s vs may_minihttp 116181.73 req/s. The example code is public, but there is no CPU model, no rustc version and no flags beyond --release, so this is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: ~15% higher requests/sec than tokio_minihttp (116,181.73 req/s vs 100,650.94 req/s; ~1.15x derived from page data)
corrections.baseline: Tokio, pre-1.0 (tokio-core 0.1 / tokio-proto 0.1 era, via tokio_minihttp)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: cargo run --example=hello-world --release; rustc version and flags not stated
corrections.caveats: First-party wrk benchmark on an unspecified laptop, single worker thread only, rustc version not stated. The baseline tokio_minihttp is built on tokio-core 0.1, tokio-proto 0.1 and futures 0.1, so the comparison is against pre-1.0 Tokio, not modern Tokio. In the independent TechEmpower R22 data (Citrine), may-minihttp beats Tokio-based hyper and axum, but Tokio-based actix-server and ntex-plt match or beat it on plaintext. may and may_minihttp are dual-licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0 (Cargo.toml 'MIT/Apache-2.0', both LICENSE files present).

notes: The numbers match the page exactly. Tier C stays: TechEmpower R22 rawData gives approximately (derived) may-minihttp 6.91M plaintext rps vs hyper 5.49M, axum 3.75M, actix-server 6.97M and ntex-plt 7.00M, and 1.205M json rps vs hyper 1.099M and actix-server 1.194M. That is framework against framework and not a clean win over Tokio, so I did not upgrade to B. The GitHub spdx is Apache-2.0, but the crate is dual-licensed, so I corrected the license.

tier_reason: BENCHMARKS.md is first-party. The bench code is public (nexus-async-web/benches/perf_async_ws.rs, which runs against tokio-tungstenite), and the CPU is stated (Core Ultra 7 165U, taskset-pinned). No rustc version or RUSTFLAGS are given, so this is C, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: TLS loopback, median of 3 runs on the tls-0.7-refactor branch: nexus-async-web on the Tokio backend + TLS takes 54 ns/msg vs 177 ns/msg for tokio-tungstenite at 40B (~3.3x) and 134 vs 280 ns/msg at 128B (~2.1x) (ratios derived from page data). The page's 'Both nexus paths are 3–5× faster' holds only with the blocking nexus-net path (37/86 ns/msg, ~4.8x/~3.3x derived). There is no nexus-async-rt row in the TLS table.
corrections.workload: WebSocket message receive throughput over TLS loopback with real syscalls, 40B and 128B payloads, wall-clock ns/msg, client and server pinned to separate physical cores (taskset -c 0,2). The page's rdtscp cycle tables use an in-memory mock transport and do not include tokio-tungstenite.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release (workspace edition 2024, MSRV 1.94); rustc version and RUSTFLAGS not stated
corrections.caveats: The cited win is protocol/codec efficiency of nexus-async-web against the tokio-tungstenite library, measured on the Tokio backend, not the nexus-async-rt event loop. Same code on nexus-async-rt vs Tokio is close to parity on the page (p50 recv 64 vs 64 cycles, send 84 vs 96 cycles, in-memory). The nexus-async-rt README says the crate is 'Experimental — not under active development' and recommends Tokio for production. Numbers come from a branch state (tls-0.7-refactor), and the nexus-async-web README gives different TLS loopback figures (34 vs 120 ns at 40B = 3.5x; 81 vs 180 ns at 128B = 2.2x). Turbo was on. No rustc version is stated.

notes: The numbers exist, but they belong to the nexus-async-web Tokio backend, not nexus-async-rt, and '3-5x' overstates the async path (128B is ~2.1x). This is really a WebSocket library entry against tokio-tungstenite rather than event-loops-io, so consider recategorizing. The metric is throughput in ns/msg, not latency. License (MIT OR Apache-2.0), last commit 2026-09-25 and 118 stars all check out.

tier_reason: README_EN.md has a first-party table (Rain 247,283 vs Tokio 219,543 req/s, Ryzen 5 5600H). The bench code is public (benchmark/echo_bench.cpp, benchmark/tokio_echo, benchmark/run_bench.sh), but the C++ compiler and version are not stated (only 'Release'), so this is C, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: ~12.6% higher requests/sec than Tokio (247,283 req/s vs 219,543 req/s; ~1.13x derived from page data); also lower max latency (9.31 ms vs 18.45 ms)
corrections.workload: Minimal loopback TCP server that writes a fixed HTTP/1.1 200 'Hello, World!' response per read (no HTTP parsing), driven by wrk -t4 -c256 -d15s on the same machine. Rain uses per-core shared-nothing loops with SO_REUSEPORT; Tokio uses the default #[tokio::main] multi-thread work-stealing runtime.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rain: CMake CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, compiler/version not stated (README requires GCC 13+ or Clang 17+); Tokio side: cargo --release with lto=true, codegen-units=1
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark with the wrk client on the same machine (loopback). The compiler and version used are not stated. There is one trivial workload: a fixed canned response, no parsing. The author attributes the win to avoiding work stealing, by relying on SO_REUSEPORT kernel balancing, against Tokio's default work-stealing runtime.

notes: The numbers match README_EN.md exactly, and the Tokio baseline source is in the repo. The 'TCP echo' label is loose: both servers return a fixed HTTP response. License MIT, 22 stars and last commit 2026-06-25 all check out.
